summary:
LunaPath is an interactive web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to simplify the exploration and comparison of potential landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole.

Our project addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by transforming published scientific research into an accessible, user-friendly platform. LunaPath allows users to explore three representative candidate sites—Slater Plain, Nobile Rim 2, and Haworth—and compare modeled sunlight availability, simultaneous Sun-and-Earth visibility, and regional terrain characteristics across the years 2025–2032.

Through interactive charts, site selection tools, and comparison tables, LunaPath makes complex lunar data easier to understand and analyze.

Our goal is to support scientific education and preliminary landing-site comparisons by making research findings more accessible to students, researchers, and space enthusiasts.

LunaPath is a research-based visualization tool, not a real-time mission simulator or a certified landing-safety system.
details:
LunaPath – Moon Landing Planner

The Challenge

Exploring potential landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole involves several important considerations, including sunlight availability, direct visibility of Earth, and surrounding terrain conditions. These factors influence opportunities for solar power generation, direct communication, and preliminary mission planning.

Although scientific research provides valuable information about these conditions, its results are often distributed across technical publications and complex datasets, making comparisons difficult for students, educators, and non-specialists.

Our Solution

LunaPath is an interactive web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It organizes published lunar research into an accessible platform that allows users to explore representative landing sites and compare important environmental characteristics.

Our solution focuses on making scientific information easier to understand through interactive exploration, visual analysis, and transparent research documentation.

How the Application Works

LunaPath features three representative sites near the lunar South Pole: Slater Plain (SP11), Nobile Rim 2 (NR2_K2023), and Haworth (HW10).

Through the Mission Explorer, users can select a site and choose a modeled year between 2025 and 2032.

The application displays representative site coordinates, regional terrain statistics, and two key visibility measurements: the maximum consecutive days of sunlight and the maximum consecutive days of simultaneous sunlight and direct Earth visibility within the modeled lunar midsummer period.

Interactive charts and comparison tables allow users to examine differences between sites and observe how the published visibility results vary across the eight studied years.

For example, during the modeled 2026 midsummer period, Slater Plain has a maximum of 18 consecutive days of simultaneous sunlight and Earth visibility, compared with 17 days for Nobile Rim 2.

Scientific Data and Sources

Our application uses structured JSON datasets containing 24 visibility records covering three sites across eight modeled years.

The scientific information is based on published research concerning lunar South Pole illumination, Earth visibility, and regional terrain characteristics. We also reference NASA’s Artemis III candidate landing-region information and lunar exploration resources.

LunaPath presents the published research results without claiming to generate new astronomical predictions.

Technology and Development

We developed LunaPath using React, Vite, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. The website combines structured scientific datasets with interactive interface components, charts, and comparison tools.

GitHub is used to manage the source code, while GitHub Pages hosts the public website.

Impact and Scientific Limitations

LunaPath helps make lunar research more approachable for students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts. It demonstrates how web technologies can transform complex scientific findings into accessible educational tools.

The application does not provide real-time illumination forecasts, calculate operational communication windows, or certify the safety of a landing site. Regional terrain statistics and modeled visibility durations support preliminary comparisons only.

Future developments could include additional sites, detailed lunar mapping, and scientifically validated astronomical simulations.

Our vision is to make lunar exploration research easier to explore, understand, and compare through an intuitive digital experience.
